name: Productivity Improvement
description: Increase labor, machine, or asset productivity.
formula: Productivity = Output / Input. Gain = (New output - Old output) × value per unit. Labor saving = headcount_reduction × cost_per_employee.
business_contexts: logistics firm rolling out route optimization software
retailer retraining store staff on new checkout process
call center deploying AI-assisted response tools
question_patterns: What is the annual value of the proposed productivity improvement?
How many FTEs could be redeployed if productivity increases by X%?
What additional output is generated with the same headcount?
Is the productivity gain large enough to justify the implementation cost?
solution_logic: Step 1: Calculate new output per worker = current_output × (1 + productivity_improvement)
Step 2: Calculate total additional output = (new_output - current_output) × number_of_workers × working_days
Step 3: Calculate revenue value of additional output = additional_output × value_per_unit
Step 4: Calculate equivalent headcount saving = improvement_pct × number_of_workers
Step 5: Calculate annual labor cost saving = headcount_saving × cost_per_worker_annual
key_insight: Productivity gains can be captured as either more output with the same headcount, or the same output with fewer people. Which the client wants determines the recommendation.
common_mistakes: Applying productivity improvement to revenue directly instead of output units
Forgetting to multiply by working days to get annual figures
Not distinguishing between output gains and cost savings — they're different recommendations
framework_soundbite: Productivity improvement has two levers: you can take it as volume or as cost. The right answer depends on whether demand exceeds supply.
